plain_english: Whatever you hope to achieve someday, you can enjoy and have right now — if you don't deny yourself your own happiness. Here's how: forget the past completely. For the future, trust in Divine Providence. Focus all your present thoughts on holiness and righteousness. Holiness means accepting willingly whatever Providence sends, knowing the universe appointed it for you, and appointed you for it. Righteousness means speaking truth freely and clearly, and doing everything justly and wisely. Don't let other people's wickedness, opinions, or words stop you from this good path. Don't let your pampered flesh stop you either — let whatever suffers look after itself. When your time comes to leave, you'll be ready to abandon everything and respect only your mind and divine part. Your only fear won't be that you'll stop living someday, but that you never started living according to nature. Then you'll truly be worthy of the world you came from. You'll stop being a stranger in your own country. You won't be amazed by daily events as if they were strange and unexpected. You won't anxiously depend on things outside your control.
original_excerpt: Whatsoever thou doest hereafter aspire unto, thou mayest even now enjoy and possess, if thou doest not envy thyself thine own happiness. And that will be, if thou shalt forget all that is past, and for the future, refer thyself wholly to the Divine Providence, and shalt bend and apply all thy present thoughts and intentions to holiness and righteousness. To holiness, in accepting willingly whatsoever is sent by the Divine Providence, as being that which the nature of the universe hath appointed unto thee, which also hath appointed thee for that, whatsoever it be. To righteousness, in speaking the truth freely, and without ambiguity; and in doing all things justly and discreetly. Now in this good course, let not other men's either wickedness, or opinion, or voice hinder thee: no, nor the sense of this thy pampered mass of flesh: for let that which suffers, look to itself. If therefore whensoever the time of thy departing shall come, thou shalt readily leave all things, and shalt respect thy mind only, and that divine part of thine, and this shall be thine only fear, not that some time or other thou shalt cease to live, but thou shalt never begin to live according to nature: then shalt thou be a man indeed, worthy of that world, from which thou hadst thy beginning; then shalt thou cease to be a stranger in thy country, and to wonder at those things that happen daily, as things strange and unexpected, and anxiously to depend of divers things that are not in thy power.

plain_english: God sees our minds and thoughts clearly, stripped of all physical covering and earthly clutter. With His pure understanding, He looks into our deepest and cleanest parts. These parts first flowed from Him like water through a pipe. If you learn to do this too, you will free yourself from all the baggage that weighs you down. When someone stops caring about their body, clothes, house, or any other external things, they find great peace and relief. There are three things that make up who you are: your body, your life, and your mind. The first two belong to you only in the sense that you must care for them. But your mind alone is truly yours.
original_excerpt: God beholds our minds and understandings, bare and naked from these material vessels, and outsides, and all earthly dross. For with His simple and pure understanding, He pierceth into our inmost and purest parts, which from His, as it were by a water pipe and channel, first flowed and issued. This if thou also shalt use to do, thou shalt rid thyself of that manifold luggage, wherewith thou art round about encumbered. For he that does regard neither his body, nor his clothing, nor his dwelling, nor any such external furniture, must needs gain unto himself great rest and ease. Three things there be in all, which thou doest consist of; thy body, thy life, and thy mind. Of these the two former, are so far forth thine, as that thou art bound to take care for them. But the third alone is that which is properly thine.

plain_english: If you can separate yourself from what other people do or say, and from what you yourself have done or said in the past, and from worrying thoughts about the future, and from everything that belongs to your body or external life that you cannot control, and from whatever random events happen to you — so that your mind stays loose and free from all these outside entanglements, always ready to let go — then your mind can live by itself and for itself, doing what is right, accepting whatever happens, and always speaking the truth. If you can separate your mind from whatever clings to it through emotion, and from all past and future time, and make yourself complete and whole like a perfect sphere, thinking only of the life you have right now — then you will be able to live the rest of your days without trouble or distraction, with nobility and generosity, in harmony with the spirit within you.
original_excerpt: If then thou shalt separate from thyself, that is from thy mind, whatsoever other men either do or say, or whatsoever thou thyself hast heretofore either done or said; and all troublesome thoughts concerning the future, and whatsoever, (as either belonging to thy body or life:) is without the jurisdiction of thine own will, and whatsoever in the ordinary course of human chances and accidents doth happen unto thee; so that thy mind (keeping herself loose and free from all outward coincidental entanglements; always in a readiness to depart:) shall live by herself, and to herself, doing that which is just, accepting whatsoever doth happen, and speaking the truth always; if, I say, thou shalt separate from thy mind, whatsoever by sympathy might adhere unto it, and all time both past and future, and shalt make thyself in all points and respects, like unto Empedocles his allegorical sphere, 'all round and circular,' &c., and shalt think of no longer life than that which is now present: then shalt thou be truly able to pass the remainder of thy days without troubles and distractions; nobly and generously disposed, and in good favour and correspondency, with that spirit which is within thee.

plain_english: I have often wondered about this strange thing. Every person loves himself most of all. Yet we care more about what others think of us than what we think of ourselves. Imagine if a god or wise teacher stood next to you. And they commanded you to think only thoughts you would speak out loud right away. No one could stand this for even one day. We fear our neighbors' opinions more than our own thoughts.
original_excerpt: I have often wondered how it should come to pass, that every man loving himself best, should more regard other men's opinions concerning himself than his own. For if any God or grave master standing by, should command any of us to think nothing by himself but what he should presently speak out; no man were able to endure it, though but for one day. Thus do we fear more what our neighbours will think of us, than what we ourselves.

plain_english: How is it that the gods, who ordered everything else so well and lovingly, would overlook just this one thing? Some very good men made promises to God. Through many holy actions they built a close relationship with Him. Yet when these men die, they are never brought back to life — they are gone forever. But you can be sure of this: if this is really how things are, the gods would never have arranged it this way unless it was right. It certainly would have been possible, if it were more just. And if it followed nature, the universe could easily have allowed it. But since it is not so (if indeed it is not), then be confident it was not meant to be. You can see this yourself — right now you are freely arguing and questioning God about this matter. But if the gods were not perfectly just and good, you would not dare reason with them this way. Since they are just and good, they could not have overlooked anything unjustly or unreasonably when they created the world.
original_excerpt: how come it to pass that the Gods having ordered all other things so well and so lovingly, should be overseen in this one only thing, that whereas then hath been some very good men that have made many covenants as it were with God and by many holy actions and outward services contracted a kind of familiarity with Him; that these men when once they are dead, should never be restored to life, but be extinct for ever. But this thou mayest be sure of, that this (if it be so indeed) would never have been so ordered by the Gods, had it been fit otherwise. For certainly it was possible, had it been more just so and had it been according to nature, the nature of the universe would easily have borne it. But now because it is not so, (if so be that it be not so indeed) be therefore confident that it was not fit it should be so for thou seest thyself, that now seeking after this matter, how freely thou doest argue and contest with God. But were not the Gods both just and good in the highest degree, thou durst not thus reason with them. Now if just and good, it could not be that in the creation of the world, they should either unjustly or unreasonably oversee anything.

plain_english: Train yourself to do even the things you think you can't do at first. Look at the left hand — it usually sits idle because we don't use it much. But it can hold the reins with more strength than the right hand, simply because it has practiced.
original_excerpt: Use thyself even unto those things that thou doest at first despair of. For the left hand we see, which for the most part lieth idle because not used; yet doth it hold the bridle with more strength than the right, because it hath been used unto it.

plain_english: Make these your daily thoughts: Think about what kind of people we should be in body and soul when death finds us. Think about how short our lives are. Think about the endless time before we were born and after we die. Think about how fragile all material things are. See all these things clearly, stripped of any false appearances. Also think about what really causes things to happen. Think about the true purpose of our actions. Think about what pain really is, what pleasure is, what death is, what fame and honor are. Remember that each person is the source of their own peace and calm. No one can truly stop you from finding that peace. Everything else is just opinion and imagination.
original_excerpt: Let these be the objects of thy ordinary meditation: to consider, what manner of men both for soul and body we ought to be, whensoever death shall surprise us: the shortness of this our mortal life: the immense vastness of the time that hath been before, and will he after us: the frailty of every worldly material object: all these things to consider, and behold clearly in themselves, all disguisement of external outside being removed and taken away. Again, to consider the efficient causes of all things: the proper ends and references of all actions: what pain is in itself; what pleasure, what death: what fame or honour, how every man is the true and proper ground of his own rest and tranquillity, and that no man can truly be hindered by any other: that all is but conceit and opinion.

plain_english: When it comes to using your principles, you should be like a fighter who uses both hands and feet, not like a gladiator with a sword. If the gladiator loses his weapon, he's finished. But the other fighter always has his hands free, which he can turn and use however he needs.
original_excerpt: As for the use of thy dogmata, thou must carry thyself in the practice of them, rather like unto a pancratiastes, or one that at the same time both fights and wrestles with hands and feet, than a gladiator. For this, if he lose his sword that he fights with, he is gone: whereas the other hath still his hand free, which he may easily turn and manage at his will.

plain_english: Look at all worldly things and break them down into three parts: what they're made of, what they look like, and what they're meant for.
original_excerpt: All worldly things thou must behold and consider, dividing them into matter, form, and reference, or their proper end.

plain_english: How wonderful that we have this power: we don't have to do anything except what is right, and we can accept whatever happens to us with peace.
original_excerpt: How happy is man in this his power that hath been granted unto him: that he needs not do anything but what God shall approve, and that he may embrace contentedly, whatsoever God doth send unto him?

plain_english: Whatever happens through the natural course of events, we shouldn't blame the gods or blame people. The gods can't do anything wrong — it's impossible for them to act badly, whether they know it or not. People only do wrong things through ignorance, so they don't really mean to. So we shouldn't blame anyone.
original_excerpt: Whatsoever doth happen in the ordinary course and consequence of natural events, neither the Gods, (for it is not possible, that they either wittingly or unwittingly should do anything amiss) nor men, (for it is through ignorance, and therefore against their wills that they do anything amiss) must be accused. None then must be accused.

plain_english: How ridiculous and strange it is to be surprised by anything that happens in the normal course of life!
original_excerpt: How ridiculous and strange is he, that wonders at anything that happens in this life in the ordinary course of nature!

plain_english: Either fate rules everything (and that means either absolute necessity that cannot be avoided, or a kind Providence that can be moved by prayer), or everything is just random chaos without order. If it's absolute necessity, why fight it? If it's a kind Providence, make yourself worthy of divine help. If it's all just chaos without anyone in charge, then you should congratulate yourself. In this flood of confusion, you have gotten a reasoning mind that can govern your own life and actions. But if you get swept away by the flood, it might be your body, or your life, or something else that belongs to them that gets swept away - not your mind and understanding. Or think of it this way: a candle flame stays bright and clear until it's blown out. Should truth, justice, and self-control stop shining in you while you still exist?
original_excerpt: Either fate, (and that either an absolute necessity, and unavoidable decree; or a placable and flexible Providence) or all is a mere casual confusion, void of all order and government. If an absolute and unavoidable necessity, why doest thou resist? If a placable and exorable Providence, make thyself worthy of the divine help and assistance. If all be a mere confusion without any moderator, or governor, then hast thou reason to congratulate thyself; that in such a general flood of confusion thou thyself hast obtained a reasonable faculty, whereby thou mayest govern thine own life and actions. But if thou beest carried away with the flood, it must be thy body perchance, or thy life, or some other thing that belongs unto them that is carried away: thy mind and understanding cannot. Or should it be so, that the light of a candle indeed is still bright and lightsome until it be put out: and should truth, and righteousness, and temperance cease to shine in thee whilest thou thyself hast any being?

plain_english: When you think someone has done wrong, ask yourself: Do I really know this is a sin? Even if it is, maybe they already feel bad about it. That would be like someone clawing at their own face — you would pity them, not get angry at them. Besides, expecting a bad person not to sin is like expecting a fig not to have juice, or a child not to cry, or a horse not to neigh. It goes against their nature. What else can they do if that's their habit? If you have the power and skill to help them change, then do it.
original_excerpt: At the conceit and apprehension that such and such a one hath sinned, thus reason with thyself; What do I know whether this be a sin indeed, as it seems to be? But if it be, what do I know but that he himself hath already condemned himself for it? And that is all one as if a man should scratch and tear his own face, an object of compassion rather than of anger. Again, that he that would not have a vicious man to sin, is like unto him that would not have moisture in the fig, nor children to welp nor a horse to neigh, nor anything else that in the course of nature is necessary. For what shall he do that hath such an habit? If thou therefore beest powerful and eloquent, remedy it if thou canst.

plain_english: If it's not right, don't do it. If it's not true, don't say it. Keep your own purpose and decisions free from all pressure and force.
original_excerpt: If it be not fitting, do it not. If it be not true, speak it not. Ever maintain thine own purpose and resolution free from all compulsion and necessity.

plain_english: With everything that comes your way, think about what it really is. Break it down: what form does it take, what is it made of, what is it actually for, and how long will it last.
original_excerpt: Of everything that presents itself unto thee, to consider what the true nature of it is, and to unfold it, as it were, by dividing it into that which is formal: that which is material: the true use or end of it, and the just time that it is appointed to last.

plain_english: It's time you understood this: there is something in you that is better and more divine than your emotions or physical desires. What is my mind focused on right now? Is it fear, suspicion, lust, or something like that? First rule: don't act rashly without a clear purpose. Second rule: have no purpose except the common good. Soon you will be gone. Soon none of the things you see now, none of the people alive today, will exist anymore. Everything is meant by nature to change, turn, and decay so other things can take their place.
original_excerpt: It is high time for thee, to understand that there is somewhat in thee, better and more divine than either thy passions, or thy sensual appetites and affections. What is now the object of my mind, is it fear, or suspicion, or lust, or any such thing? To do nothing rashly without some certain end; let that be thy first care. The next, to have no other end than the common good. For, alas! yet a little while, and thou art no more: no more will any, either of those things that now thou seest, or of those men that now are living, be any more. For all things are by nature appointed soon to be changed, turned, and corrupted, that other things might succeed in their room.

plain_english: Remember that everything is just opinion. All opinion comes from the mind. Take away your opinion, and you have instant calm — like a ship that has sailed safely into harbor. Everything becomes safe and steady. You reach a peaceful bay that no storm can touch.
original_excerpt: Remember that all is but opinion, and all opinion depends of the mind. Take thine opinion away, and then as a ship that hath stricken in within the arms and mouth of the harbour, a present calm; all things safe and steady: a bay, not capable of any storms and tempests: as the poet hath it.

plain_english: When any action stops for a while, no one can truly say the person doing it suffers any harm just because it ended. The person who was doing the action doesn't suffer harm either, simply because the action is finished. In the same way, when our whole series of actions — which is our life — comes to an end in time, it can't be said to suffer harm just because it's over. And the person who brought this series of actions to a close can't truly be said to have been harmed.
original_excerpt: No operation whatsoever it he, ceasing for a while, can be truly said to suffer any evil, because it is at an end. Neither can he that is the author of that operation; for this very respect, because his operation is at an end, be said to suffer any evil. Likewise then, neither can the whole body of all our actions (which is our life) if in time it cease, be said to suffer any evil for this very reason, because it is at an end; nor he truly be said to have been ill affected, that did put a period to this series of actions.

plain_english: This time we have — this certain period — depends on how nature decides. Sometimes it's particular nature, like when someone dies old. But it's also nature in general. The parts keep changing one after another, but the whole world stays fresh and new. What's best and most fitting is always what's good for the whole. So death itself can't hurt anyone in particular. It's not shameful. It doesn't depend on our will, and it's not against the common good. In general, death is both useful and timely for the whole. In that way, it must be good. Death comes to us through the order of Divine Providence. So when someone's will and mind go along with divine order — when their will matches Divine Providence — they are led and driven by God himself. That person can truly be called divinely led and inspired.
original_excerpt: Now this time or certain period, depends of the determination of nature: sometimes of particular nature, as when a man dieth old; but of nature in general, however; the parts whereof thus changing one after another, the whole world still continues fresh and new. Now that is ever best and most seasonable, which is for the good of the whole. Thus it appears that death of itself can neither be hurtful to any in particular, because it is not a shameful thing (for neither is it a thing that depends of our own will, nor of itself contrary to the common good) and generally, as it is both expedient and seasonable to the whole, that in that respect it must needs be good. It is that also, which is brought unto us by the order and appointment of the Divine Providence; so that he whose will and mind in these things runs along with the Divine ordinance, and by this concurrence of his will and mind with the Divine Providence, is led and driven along, as it were by God Himself; may truly be termed and esteemed the θεοφόρητος, or divinely led and inspired.

plain_english: Keep three things always ready in your mind: First, about your own actions — make sure you do nothing without purpose, and nothing that goes against what is right and fair. Second, about things that happen to you from outside — they come either by chance or by providence. It makes no sense to blame either one.
original_excerpt: These three things thou must have always in a readiness: first concerning thine own actions, whether thou doest nothing either idly, or otherwise, than justice and equity do require: and concerning those things that happen unto thee externally, that either they happen unto thee by chance, or by providence; of which two to accuse either, is equally against reason.

plain_english: Second, consider what our bodies are like while they are still crude and unformed, until they come to life. And from when they come alive until they die: what they are made of, and what they will break down into.
original_excerpt: Secondly, what like unto our bodies are whilest yet rude and imperfect, until they be animated: and from their animation, until their expiration: of what things they are compounded, and into what things they shall be dissolved.

plain_english: Third, see how empty all things will look when you step back and view everything on earth from above. Notice how everything changes constantly. Think about the vast size and endless variety of things in the air and sky around us. Every time you look at these things, you'll see the same pattern. The same things, the same brief existence. And yet these are the things we get so proud and puffed up about.
original_excerpt: Thirdly, how vain all things will appear unto thee when, from on high as it were, looking down thou shalt contemplate all things upon earth, and the wonderful mutability, that they are subject unto: considering withal, the infinite both greatness and variety of things aerial and things celestial that are round about it. And that as often as thou shalt behold them, thou shalt still see the same: as the same things, so the same shortness of continuance of all those things. And, behold, these be the things that we are so proud and puffed up for.

plain_english: Drop your opinion, and you are safe. What stops you from dropping it? When something upsets you, have you forgotten that all things happen according to the nature of the universe? That only the person at fault should be concerned? And that what happens now has always happened in the world, and will always happen, and is happening everywhere right now? How closely all people are connected to each other — not by blood or birth, but by sharing the same kind of mind.
original_excerpt: Cast away from thee opinion, and thou art safe. And what is it that hinders thee from casting of it away? When thou art grieved at anything, hast thou forgotten that all things happen according to the nature of the universe; and that him only it concerns, who is in fault; and moreover, that what is now done, is that which from ever hath been done in the world, and will ever be done, and is now done everywhere: how nearly all men are allied one to another by a kindred not of blood, nor of seed, but of the same mind.

plain_english: You have also forgotten that every person's mind shares in something divine. Nothing truly belongs to us — not our children, not our bodies, not our lives. Everything comes from the same source. All things are just opinions. No one really lives except in this present moment. So when someone dies, they lose nothing more than an instant of time.
original_excerpt: Thou hast also forgotten that every man's mind partakes of the Deity, and issueth from thence; and that no man can properly call anything his own, no not his son, nor his body, nor his life; for that they all proceed from that One who is the giver of all things: that all things are but opinion; that no man lives properly, but that very instant of time which is now present. And therefore that no man whensoever he dieth can properly be said to lose any more, than an instant of time.

plain_english: Think about people who were once filled with rage over something. People who reached the heights of fame or fell into disaster. People consumed by hatred and feuds. People caught up in any kind of fortune or trouble. Now look what happened to all of that. It all turned to smoke and ash. It became nothing more than a story — maybe not even that. Think of men like Fabius Catulinus in battle, or Lucius Lupus and Stertinius at Baiae, or Tiberius at Capri, or Velius Rufus. All of them threw themselves into worldly pursuits with such intensity. Keep these examples in mind. See how worthless the things they chased so desperately really were. How much better it is to handle whatever comes your way with justice and balance. To follow the gods with simple honesty. The worst kind of pride is being proud that you're not proud.
original_excerpt: Let thy thoughts ever run upon them, who once for some one thing or other, were moved with extraordinary indignation; who were once in the highest pitch of either honour, or calamity; or mutual hatred and enmity; or of any other fortune or condition whatsoever. Then consider what's now become of all those things. All is turned to smoke; all to ashes, and a mere fable; and perchance not so much as a fable. As also whatsoever is of this nature, as Fabius Catulinus in the field; Lucius Lupus, and Stertinius, at Baiæ Tiberius at Capreæ and Velius Rufus, and all such examples of vehement prosecution in worldly matters; let these also run in thy mind at the same time; and how vile every object of such earnest and vehement prosecution is; and how much more agreeable to true philosophy it is, for a man to carry himself in every matter that offers itself; justly, and moderately, as one that followeth the Gods with all simplicity. For, for a man to be proud and high conceited, that he is not proud and high conceited, is of all kind of pride and presumption, the most intolerable.

plain_english: To those who ask you, "Where have you seen the Gods? How do you know for certain that Gods exist, that you worship them so faithfully?" I answer first that they are visible in some way, even to the eye. Second, I have never seen my own soul, yet I respect and honor it. So with the Gods — through daily experience of their power and care for myself and others, I know certainly that they exist. That is why I worship them.
original_excerpt: To them that ask thee, Where hast thou seen the Gods, or how knowest thou certainly that there be Gods, that thou art so devout in their worship? I answer first of all, that even to the very eye, they are in some manner visible and apparent. Secondly, neither have I ever seen mine own soul, and yet I respect and honour it. So then for the Gods, by the daily experience that I have of their power and providence towards myself and others, I know certainly that they are, and therefore worship them.

plain_english: Here is what makes life happy: to understand the true nature of everything — what it's made of and how it's shaped. To do what is right with all your heart and soul, and to speak the truth. What's left then but to enjoy your life through a steady stream of good actions, one right after another, never broken even for a moment?
original_excerpt: Herein doth consist happiness of life, for a man to know thoroughly the true nature of everything; what is the matter, and what is the form of it: with all his heart and soul, ever to do that which is just, and to speak the truth. What then remaineth but to enjoy thy life in a course and coherence of good actions, one upon another immediately succeeding, and never interrupted, though for never so little a while?

plain_english:
There is only one sun, even though walls and mountains and countless other things block its light. There is only one substance that makes up the whole world, even though it gets packed into countless different bodies. There is only one common soul, even though it gets divided into countless individual essences and natures. So there is only one shared mind, even though it seems divided.

As for the other parts of these universal things I mentioned — like the senses or physical objects — these have no natural connection to each other (since they lack reason), even though many contain a mind that rules them. But every thinking mind has this special nature: it seeks out others like itself and wants to be united with them. This shared longing for connection cannot be blocked or divided or limited to individuals the way those other universal things can be.
original_excerpt: There is but one light of the sun, though it be intercepted by walls and mountains, and other thousand objects. There is but one common substance of the whole world, though it be concluded and restrained into several different bodies, in number infinite. There is but one common soul, though divided into innumerable particular essences and natures. So is there but one common intellectual soul, though it seem to be divided. And as for all other parts of those generals which we have mentioned, as either sensitive souls or subjects, these of themselves (as naturally irrational) have no common mutual reference one unto another, though many of them contain a mind, or reasonable faculty in them, whereby they are ruled and governed. But of every reasonable mind, this the particular nature, that it hath reference to whatsoever is of her own kind, and desireth to be united: neither can this common affection, or mutual unity and correspondency, be here intercepted or divided, or confined to particulars as those other common things are.

plain_english: What do you want? To live long. But what does that mean? To feel things? To want things? To grow up and then get old? To be able to talk and think for a long time? Which of these seems worth wanting? If you look closely, none of these things matter much by themselves. So focus on what does matter: following God and reason in everything. It goes against both God and reason to grieve that death will take these things away.
original_excerpt: What doest thou desire? To live long. What? To enjoy the operations of a sensitive soul; or of the appetitive faculty? or wouldst thou grow, and then decrease again? Wouldst thou long be able to talk, to think and reason with thyself? Which of all these seems unto thee a worthy object of thy desire? Now if of all these thou doest find that they be but little worth in themselves, proceed on unto the last, which is, in all things to follow God and reason. But for a man to grieve that by death he shall be deprived of any of these things, is both against God and reason.

plain_english: What a tiny slice of endless time each of us gets, and how quickly it disappears into the history of the world. What a small piece of the common substance we are given, and of the shared soul too. And what a tiny speck of the whole earth we crawl around on. After you think about these things clearly, don't imagine that anything else in the world has real importance. Only this matters: do what your own nature requires, and accept what the common nature provides.
original_excerpt: What a small portion of vast and infinite eternity it is, that is allowed unto every one of us, and how soon it vanisheth into the general age of the world: of the common substance, and of the common soul also what a small portion is allotted unto us: and in what a little clod of the whole earth (as it were) it is that thou doest crawl. After thou shalt rightly have considered these things with thyself; fancy not anything else in the world any more to be of any weight and moment but this, to do that only which thine own nature doth require; and to conform thyself to that which the common nature doth afford.

plain_english: What is the current state of my mind? This is what really matters. Everything else is beyond my control. And if it's beyond my control, then it's dead to me — like smoke that drifts away.
original_excerpt: What is the present estate of my understanding? For herein lieth all indeed. As for all other things, they are without the compass of mine own will: and if without the compass of my will, then are they as dead things unto me, and as it were mere smoke.

plain_english: Here's something that helps you face death without fear: even people who lived only for pleasure and hated pain often faced death bravely. So how can death be terrible to you? You think something is good only when it comes at the right time in nature's course. It makes no difference to you whether you do many good deeds or just a few, as long as they're all good. And you don't care whether you see the world for many years or just a few — the world stays the same either way.
original_excerpt: To stir up a man to the contempt of death this among other things, is of good power and efficacy, that even they who esteemed pleasure to be happiness, and pain misery, did nevertheless many of them contemn death as much as any. And can death be terrible to him, to whom that only seems good, which in the ordinary course of nature is seasonable? to him, to whom, whether his actions be many or few, so they be all good, is all one; and who whether he behold the things of the world being always the same either for many years, or for few years only, is altogether indifferent?

plain_english: You have lived as a citizen in this great city — the world. Whether for many years or few, what does it matter? You have lived as long as the natural order required. This should comfort everyone. Why should it upset you when the same nature that brought you into the world now calls you to leave? It's like a judge fairly dismissing an actor from the stage after his performance. "But the play isn't finished! Only three acts have been performed!" True — but in life, three acts is the whole play. Only the one who created you and now dissolves you gets to decide how long each person performs. You have nothing to do with either. So go peacefully and content. That's how the one dismissing you wants it.
original_excerpt: O man! as a citizen thou hast lived, and conversed in this great city the world. Whether just for so many years, or no, what is it unto thee? Thou hast lived (thou mayest be sure) as long as the laws and orders of the city required; which may be the common comfort of all. Why then should it be grievous unto thee, if (not a tyrant, nor an unjust judge, but) the same nature that brought thee in, doth now send thee out of the world? As if the praetor should fairly dismiss him from the stage, whom he had taken in to act a while. Oh, but the play is not yet at an end, there are but three acts yet acted of it? Thou hast well said: for in matter of life, three acts is the whole play. Now to set a certain time to every man's acting, belongs unto him only, who as first he was of thy composition, so is now the cause of thy dissolution. As for thyself; thou hast to do with neither. Go thy ways then well pleased and contented: for so is He that dismisseth thee.
